Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 3):

The question is: what is faith (iman)? ... We do not here give a jurisprudential (fiqhi) explanation or definition of faith. Our discussion is limited to the nature of faith, its value, and its effects on life.

Faith is in fact the bond which this small, limited, human creature establishes with the Reality that is eternal, everlasting and abiding, which is the origin of this universe and from which this universe has come into being. For this reason, this human creature becomes connected, in that respect, with the universe as well, because the Creator of both is one. Then this human being becomes connected with the laws of nature according to which this world operates, and the human being becomes connected with the forces that are at work in this universe, and the human being emerges from the shell of his petty and limited self and enters into the vastness of the universe. Thus he goes beyond the limits of his restricted power and enters those "unlimited forces" that exist within this universe. And this universe is so vast in comparison with the human being that its boundaries themselves lie outside the human being's knowledge. Then the human being goes beyond the circle of his limited lifespan and enters the unlimited times of the Resurrection and the ages that come after it.

This connection of the human creature, which grants it such strength, such vastness and such freedom, at the same time also grants it the taste to enjoy this entire universe and its beauty and grace, and to see the creatures that love its soul. Because of this connection, the brief journey of life becomes for the human being a journey of recreation, or a stroll through an exhibition which Allah has adorned for this human being in every place, every spot and every era. The truth is that this is a very great good fortune, a supreme kind of joy and recreation, and a friendship with this entire universe, and it is a wealth in comparison with which no other wealth has any value. It is also a loss such that if anyone is deprived of it, there is no greater loss or deficit than this.

Then, the basic elements of faith are also those that are the basic constituent elements of humanity:

(1) Through the servitude of one God, the human being is freed from all obedience, servitude and worship other than the one true God. Thus there arises within human beings the concept that all servants hold one station and are equal to one another. Therefore it is not a reasonable attitude that a human being should be granted the true blessing of freedom! That is the freedom which springs from the human conscience and springs from a concept that exists as an actual reality, and that concept is that in this universe there is only one real power and one real object of worship. Therefore the natural demand of this conception of life and conception of the universe is that the human being be free, and the logical result of this belief is also that the human being be free.

(2) The human being acquires a divine character (rabbaniyyah), and derives all his concepts, all his values and standards, all his priorities, and his entire constitution and law from Allah. His relationships with Allah, with this universe and with people are established according to the commands and laws of Allah. His personal desires and personal interests disappear from his life, and in their place the Shariah of Allah and justice take their place. In the consciousness of the believer, the value of his system of life becomes elevated; his personality rises above the concepts and values of jahiliyyah. Jahili priorities come to an end, and all those connections come to an end which are based on the earth, this world and materialistic concepts. Even if this human being is an individual, because an individual believer also takes his concepts, his values and his priorities directly from Allah, since these values are indeed more exalted, more honourable, and more beneficial and worthy of consideration.

(3) As a result of faith, the relationship between Creator and creature is also determined. The station of lordship and servitude, of divinity and worship, is also determined, and this relationship emerges clear and pure. This relationship, which joins a mortal human being to an immortal Being, becomes determined and clear in a very simple and comprehensible manner, and on this path the human being has no need of any intermediary. The determination of ranks produces light in the heart and tranquillity in the spirit. Love and trust arise in the human soul. Doubt, fear, anguish and restlessness come to an end. Through this clarity of ranks, the human being does not commit unjust arrogance, nor does he, by fabricating falsehoods and relying on invented concepts, claim for himself an exalted status over other human beings.

(4) Because of faith, the People of Faith are granted steadfastness upon the Islamic system of life. Therefore goodness among the believers is not a temporary matter, nor is it an accidental, isolated event; rather, the Islamic system is an occurrence that has real causes and has certain real objectives, and those who run the Islamic system are people connected with one another for the sake of Allah, who support one another, and from such people a sound community is formed, which has one single aim and one distinctive banner. This community is a historical community, and its past generations are also connected with the generations to come, and the generations to come are connected with the past, and this connection is a strong connection.

(5) As a result of this, a concept arises among people that the human being is exceedingly honoured. The human being rises high in his own eyes, and in the conscience of the believer there arises the modesty that he should not do any act as a result of which he would fall from the station to which Allah has raised him, and this is that lofty and exalted station which no human being could imagine reaching: that he is honoured in the sight of Allah. Every religion or philosophical concept that lowers the human being in his own eyes and declares him a contemptible creature who has come into being in a sinful manner, creates distance between the human being and the higher realm. Such a religion or philosophy degrades the human being and leads him towards degradation, even if it does not say so explicitly.

Thus the philosophies of Darwin and Freud and the Marxist system were the worst philosophies and systems, which afflicted the human being with the worst calamity, gave him a wrong direction in terms of humanity, nature and human dignity, and made him believe that every degradation, every filth and every contempt is in fact a natural and necessary part of human life. This is not even a matter for surprise, therefore there is nothing in it to be ashamed of. Thus these philosophies and systems are in fact a heinous crime against humanity and deserve to be hated. (Sayyid, do you know that news has reached you that all the idols of Marxism have been toppled from the socialist world?)

(6) The mere concept that the human being is a noble creature in the sight of Allah purifies and cleanses human consciousness. Then the concept that Allah is the overseer of all and that He is Knower of what is in the breasts (Alim bi-dhat al-sudur) also purifies human consciousness. A naturally sound human being whose nature has not been distorted by the writings of people like Karl Marx and Freud feels shame at the thought that another human being like himself should be informed of the secrets of his heart and his evil thoughts. And a true believer, who holds firm conviction that Allah is aware of all the secrets and hidden things in his breast, trembles at the thought that such and such thoughts are in his heart. Through this he purifies his consciousness, his feelings, and also cleanses his heart.

The truth is that the moment faith arises, a moral beauty arises within the human being. He believes that there is one God who is just, merciful, generous and forgiving, forbearing and loving; He does not like evil, He likes goodness. He knows the treachery of the eyes and the one who knows the secrets of hearts.

(7) Then the concept that the human being has been given freedom of will, and at the same time he is under complete observation by Allah, and as a result of this, awareness and alertness arise within a person, and the understanding and reflection that arise as a result make the human being see himself as a responsible being, and it is the right of every good that through it the human being adopts a responsible attitude and also feels a sense of responsibility towards other human beings. And this responsibility is before Allah. Therefore, when a believer makes any movement, his awareness and consciousness is such that in every matter and at every step he thinks in his heart and reflects upon the consequences before taking a step. Because according to this concept the human being is a creature that holds a position in this world; therefore, in the order of this universe he is a responsible creature.

(8) One important effect among the effects of faith is that a believer does not pounce upon the interests of the world in the way that dogs pounce upon bones. Among the signals and effects of faith is that he adopts that which holds high purpose in the sight of Allah, and which is "good" and abiding.

And in that [regard] let the competitors compete (83:26) — "Let those who compete, compete in goodness." Competition among the rewards of Allah elevates the human being above this world, purifies his heart, and the human being becomes clean and pure. Also, through this the sphere of a believer's activities becomes wide. He goes beyond the boundaries of the world and is active in the Hereafter as well. Along with the earth, he displays his prowess in the higher realm. And this very thing creates in him the strength to continue doing good without regard for results, or not to be hasty about results. Because he seeks goodness because it is goodness and because the pleasure of Allah is so; it is not his responsibility that the results of goodness should also emerge within this small, limited lifespan. Because the Allah for whose sake this goodness is being done is living; He does not die. He does not forget, He is not heedless of anything. Moreover, this world is not the true abode of recompense, and not all accounts are settled in this world. Therefore the believer seeks help for continuing goodness from the spring which never dries up, and this is why the movement of goodness continues. It is not a momentary enthusiasm, nor an individual incident. It is precisely this faithful impulse because of which a believer develops such strength that he stands against the greatest evil, whether this evil takes the form of a single dictator and rebel, or the pressure of jahili concepts and priorities, or the form of the desires of the self. This individual pressure falls upon a person in such a way that he thinks this world is brief, life is short, and one should enjoy luxury in it:

Babur ba-aish kosh, ki alam dobara nist (Babur, enjoy life, for the world does not come again)

Or he thinks that it is so brief that good outcomes cannot emerge within it, and that the prospect of seeing truth prevail over falsehood is not visible to us. Therefore faith treats this condition, and treats it at its root.

The truth is that faith alone is the foundation of life, the root of life, and from it all the branches of goodness sprout, and each of its fruits depends upon these roots. And if there is no faith, it is as though the root of the tree has been cut, and all its branches will wither and dry up; and if they do not dry up, then that will be a satanic fruit, and it will not attain permanence or growth.

The truth is that faith is the center and axis to which all the strings of higher life are connected, and if there is no faith, life is an unconnected movement, and without faith this life has no stability or permanence. Desires and inclinations pull a person wherever they go.

Faith is in fact a system, and because of it all scattered deeds become connected with one another, and because of it these deeds come into harmony with one another; they are oriented in one direction, having one movement, one motivation, and one goal.

For this reason the Holy Qur'an declares null every deed that is not based upon this principle, that does not revolve around this axis, and does not spring from the fountainhead of faith. The Islamic worldview and Islamic system of belief are completely open and explicit in this matter. In Surah Ibrahim there is:

"The likeness of those who disbelieved in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows hard on a stormy day; they will not be able to obtain anything of what they have earned" (14:18). And in Surah al-Nur:

"And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing" (24:39). These texts clearly show that deeds, as long as they are not based on faith, have no value in Islam. The motive beneath deeds should be that the Creator of the universe has commanded them, and their purpose should be to harmonize with the creation of this universe. And this is the logical consequence of the belief which returns all affairs to Allah; therefore, any deed whose connection with faith has been severed has lost its meaning and value. (Ustadh Muhammad Abduh, under the verse "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (8:99), wrote that "some scholars have recorded a consensus that no good deed of a disbeliever will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection and his punishment will not be lightened, but this is a fundamental matter.") We hold that this issue is not one of consensus but of the explicit texts of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an and Sunnah are completely clear in this matter. (Sayyid Qutb)

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 2 of 3):

Faith is evidence that the believer's nature is sound, that the structure of his personality is correct and whole, and that he is in harmony with this entire universe. The nature found in his environment is in accord with the universe, and therefore he lives in this universe [in peace]. The personality of a believer who is sound has a correspondence with the universe, and this correspondence and unity is purely the fruit of faith, because in this universe there are such proofs and signs which indicate that one and the same Hand of Power is the Creator of the universe. Therefore, if this correspondence between man and the universe is severed, this will be evidence that a disorder has entered the personality of that man and that the capacity by which he derives proofs and signs from the universe has been destroyed. Because of this corruption, man will remain in loss. Although some deeds may appear to bear the stamp of goodness, because of the absence of faith these deeds will be unacceptable.... In short, the world of the believer is broad, comprehensive, long, lofty, beautiful and successful. In contrast, the world of those who are not believers is small, despicable, fallen, weak, hopeless and wretched, and its outcome and end is loss and failure.

*Wa 'amilu al-salihat* (3:103): "and they do righteous deeds." Righteous deeds are in reality the natural fruit of faith, and when faith settles in a heart, righteous action is its inherent movement (just as the heart is in motion). Therefore faith is the name of a dynamic and positive movement; as soon as it settles in a personality, it appears in the form of righteous action. From the Islamic point of view, faith is exactly this. In Islam there is no concept of a faith that is extinguished and from which no movement arises, a faith that is hidden and does not come out from the believer's self in living form. If there is no such natural movement within it, that faith is counterfeit and dead faith. Faith is like a flower whose fragrance cannot be restrained: wherever there is a flower, its fragrance will continue to spread. And if a person has no scent of faith, then it is as though he does not exist.

From this it becomes clear that faith is the name of movement, action and construction, and all these matters are directed from Allah. There is no contraction in faith, nor is it a negative thing. Nor does it settle in the folds of conscience. Faith is not the name of good wishes that have no movement behind them. This is the open temperament of Islam, which makes Islam a lofty constructive force, and this power is the central driving force within practical life.

This is the meaning of the principle that faith must be connected with the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of life, since it is the name of a continuous movement which is proceeding throughout this entire universe, and this movement has been created by a governing power, and it has a goal. Entrusting the leadership of humanity to faith means bringing into existence a leadership which produces a method of movement that is in accordance with the temperament of this entire universe; in other words, establishing a good, pure constructive struggle that is worthy of the system of life sent down by Allah.

*Wa tawasaw* ... *bi-al-sabr* (3:103): "who enjoin one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience." From the practice of enjoining truth and enjoining patience, the features of the Muslim community become clearly apparent. A united community (jama'ah muslimah) is also formed along the lines of the Muslim community. It has a distinct existence and personality. Its members have a distinctive bond among themselves. All people share one direction; this community or group has awareness of its own existence, and its duties are also before it, and this community knows what it has to do in respect of faith and righteous action; and it knows that it has to lead the whole of humanity from the standpoint of faith and righteous action. Therefore, enjoining one another to truth means that you must take up the great trust.

In short, from the word *tawasi* and from its meaning, its essence and its temperament, the existence of the Muslim community emerges, or the concept of a united community arises. That is, a community that is distinguished, wise, and responsible for establishing truth, goodness and justice on this earth. Thus this is the most exalted and beautiful picture of the Muslim community. Islam desires such a community: a distinguished, strong, wise community that watches over truth and goodness, whose members constantly advise one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience, who live together in mutual love and cooperation, and among whom a special brotherhood prevails, which the Qur'an calls *wasiyyah* (mutual counsel).

Enjoining truth is necessary because carrying the truth is a difficult task; in this world there are countless factors that lead a person away from the path of truth: carnal desires, expediencies, national and family notions, the oppression of rebels and dictators, the injustice of oppressors, the transgressions and aggressions of those who exceed limits, and so on. By advising one another, in fact, reminders take place; people's resolve increases, and unity and harmony arise among the members of the group with respect to aims and objectives. And in bearing responsibilities, in fact, one carries another's burden. Through advice, all individual inclinations gather together and multiply many times over, and all those who are guardians and supporters of truth feel that they are not alone: in the task of protecting truth and righteousness there are others with them, who advise them, encourage them, love them, and stand behind them, and who will never let them be put to shame. This religion is indeed the truth, and only a community can protect this religion, a community that is mutually acquainted, mutually supportive, mutually helpful, and that makes up for one another's weaknesses.

And enjoining patience is also very necessary, because remaining on the path of faith and righteous action and watching over truth and justice is a difficult task. It requires patience, perseverance, and a fierce struggle against the factors within the self, and it also requires struggle against the factors outside the self, and there is need for endurance and hardship in the face of difficulties that come in this path. Likewise, it means being patient with the arrogance and pride of falsehood, being patient with the length of the road, being patient with the slowness of success, and with the effacement and disappearance of the signposts of the path, and being patient with them.

Through the enjoining of patience, human strength increases, and a collective feeling arises among people that all of us have a single goal and one direction; thus everyone finds a support in it. Workers, while working on this path, become close and united, and they advance with great resolve, steadfastness and insistence on their aim. Moreover, through it many other collective qualities also come into being, and these are necessary for the stability of an Islamic community, because Islam cannot live without a communal atmosphere. Islam's manifestation also takes the form of a society. If there is no society at all, Islam will not exist, and that would be a clear loss.

The Qur'an has set down for us a constitution by which a society is declared successful and protected from worldly and otherworldly loss. If we look at the present conditions of the world through the lens of this constitution, before us will appear this frightening picture of the world: that at this time the whole world is in complete loss. The more frightening aspect of this loss is that even before the Hereafter, we have fallen into severe loss from a purely worldly standpoint. We see that humanity has completely turned away from that goodness whose blessings and bounties Allah had made general for human beings. Moreover, from this world that sovereign authority has disappeared which is faithful and Islamic, which is founded upon the principles of goodness, truth and justice. The most unsightly aspect of this picture is that Muslims, or, to use more accurate words, those people who in comparison to the other inhabitants of this earth have fallen very far from that goodness and virtue, have gone very far from the system of life which Allah had chosen for them. They have trampled underfoot the constitution and law which Allah had prescribed for them, which Allah had declared to be the only path to salvation from loss and failure. Especially those regions from which the banners of this goodness were first raised: they themselves have brought down those banners which Allah had raised for them. These were the banners of faith. And the most unfortunate thing is that the regions from which the banners of Allah's religion were raised have adopted racial nationalism, although the history of this earth bears witness that through racial nationalism no nation has ever reached goodness. The racial nationalism (Arab nationalism) whose banners these people have raised existed among them even before Islam, but because of it they neither accomplished any notable feat on this earth, nor was any achievement of theirs recorded in the heavens. When Islam came, through the Arabs it raised a banner which was purely the banner of Allah; no other element shared in it. It was in the name of Allah; no one shared in the name; it was attributed to Allah alone, with no other attribution; it had only the colour of Allah and no other colour. Under the shade of this banner the Arabs attained ascendancy; they became the leaders of the world. And their leadership was the leadership of goodness: it was a strong leadership, a wise leadership, and a successful leadership from every aspect. This achievement succeeded for the first time in Arab history, and also in human history the Islamic revolution was a notable success for humanity.

Maulana Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in the chapter "Islamic Power and Muslim Leaders" of his famous book *Insani Duniya par Musalmanon ka Urooj-o-Zawal ka Asar* (The Effect of the Rise and Fall of the Muslims on the Human World), says:

"The Muslims came onto the field, took into their hands the reins of guiding the world, and removed from that office of guidance those sick nations which had seized it and which they had never used properly. The Muslims took the whole of humanity with them and began to lead it, with balance and right pace, toward its correct destination. In them were gathered all those qualities which proved them worthy of the exalted office of guiding all nations, and which, under their watch and leadership, guaranteed the welfare and felicity of nations. What were those distinctive qualities? They are these:

(1) They had the heavenly Book and the Shariah of God; they did not legislate on their own. For human legislation is a fountain of ignorance, oppression and error, and when humans make laws for humans, changes and amendments keep occurring in them every day, whereas heavenly books are protected from such errors. The Muslims were safe from blindly walking in their daily affairs, in politics and in leadership, and from groping in darkness. They had the light of divine revelation by which they walked, and by which all the paths and turns of life were lit for them. Every step they took fell in light, and they could clearly see their destination. In Surah al-An'am (6:122) it is said:

'Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, unable to emerge from it?'

They had a divine law and Shariah by which they judged between people. They were made standard-bearers of truth and justice, and they were commanded, even in the state of the strongest provocation, anger, enmity and hatred, not to abandon truth and justice, and not to take revenge in matters of truth and justice:

'O you who believe, be steadfast for Allah, witnesses in justice; and let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do' (5:8).

(2) They attained to rule and leadership after firm moral training and refinement of the soul. They did not leap from the depths to the heights with all the moral defects and flaws of the common ruling peoples of the world. Rather, for a long period divine revelation kept reforming and training them, and for years they were under the complete supervision and instruction of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He purified them and fully trained them. He made them accustomed to a life of asceticism and piety, and instilled in them chastity, trustworthiness, selflessness and sacrifice, and fear of God. He completely removed from their hearts greed and desire for rule and offices. His saying was: 'By God, we shall never entrust an office to one who asks for it or who desires it.' Their hearts were entirely purified of the wish for ascendancy, eminence and honour, and of the desire for strife and corruption; and in their ears, day and night, these words of the Qur'an resounded:

'That is the Abode of the Hereafter; We grant it to those who do not desire superiority on earth or corruption, and the best outcome is for the righteous' (28:83)."

Along with the earth, he displays his prowess in the higher realm. And this very thing creates in him the strength to continue doing good without regard for results, or not to be hasty about results. Because he seeks goodness because it is goodness and because the pleasure of Allah is so; it is not his responsibility that the results of goodness should also emerge within this small, limited lifespan. Therefore the believer seeks help for continuing goodness from the spring which never dries up, and this is why the movement of goodness continues. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 2 of 3):

Faith is evidence that the believer's nature is sound, that the structure of his personality is correct and whole, and that he is in harmony with this entire universe. The nature found in his environment is in accord with the universe, and therefore he lives in this universe [in peace]. The personality of a believer who is sound has a correspondence with the universe, and this correspondence and unity is purely the fruit of faith, because in this universe there are such proofs and signs which indicate that one and the same Hand of Power is the Creator of the universe. Therefore, if this correspondence between man and the universe is severed, this will be evidence that a disorder has entered the personality of that man and that the capacity by which he derives proofs and signs from the universe has been destroyed. Because of this corruption, man will remain in loss. Although some deeds may appear to bear the stamp of goodness, because of the absence of faith these deeds will be unacceptable.... In short, the world of the believer is broad, comprehensive, long, lofty, beautiful and successful. In contrast, the world of those who are not believers is small, despicable, fallen, weak, hopeless and wretched, and its outcome and end is loss and failure.

*Wa 'amilu al-salihat* (3:103): "and they do righteous deeds." Righteous deeds are in reality the natural fruit of faith, and when faith settles in a heart, righteous action is its inherent movement (just as the heart is in motion). Therefore faith is the name of a dynamic and positive movement; as soon as it settles in a personality, it appears in the form of righteous action. From the Islamic point of view, faith is exactly this. In Islam there is no concept of a faith that is extinguished and from which no movement arises, a faith that is hidden and does not come out from the believer's self in living form. If there is no such natural movement within it, that faith is counterfeit and dead faith. Faith is like a flower whose fragrance cannot be restrained: wherever there is a flower, its fragrance will continue to spread. And if a person has no scent of faith, then it is as though he does not exist.

From this it becomes clear that faith is the name of movement, action and construction, and all these matters are directed from Allah. There is no contraction in faith, nor is it a negative thing. Nor does it settle in the folds of conscience. Faith is not the name of good wishes that have no movement behind them. This is the open temperament of Islam, which makes Islam a lofty constructive force, and this power is the central driving force within practical life.

This is the meaning of the principle that faith must be connected with the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of life, since it is the name of a continuous movement which is proceeding throughout this entire universe, and this movement has been created by a governing power, and it has a goal. Entrusting the leadership of humanity to faith means bringing into existence a leadership which produces a method of movement that is in accordance with the temperament of this entire universe; in other words, establishing a good, pure constructive struggle that is worthy of the system of life sent down by Allah.

*Wa tawasaw* ... *bi-al-sabr* (3:103): "who enjoin one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience." From the practice of enjoining truth and enjoining patience, the features of the Muslim community become clearly apparent. A united community (jama'ah muslimah) is also formed along the lines of the Muslim community. It has a distinct existence and personality. Its members have a distinctive bond among themselves. All people share one direction; this community or group has awareness of its own existence, and its duties are also before it, and this community knows what it has to do in respect of faith and righteous action; and it knows that it has to lead the whole of humanity from the standpoint of faith and righteous action. Therefore, enjoining one another to truth means that you must take up the great trust.

In short, from the word *tawasi* and from its meaning, its essence and its temperament, the existence of the Muslim community emerges, or the concept of a united community arises. That is, a community that is distinguished, wise, and responsible for establishing truth, goodness and justice on this earth. Thus this is the most exalted and beautiful picture of the Muslim community. Islam desires such a community: a distinguished, strong, wise community that watches over truth and goodness, whose members constantly advise one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience, who live together in mutual love and cooperation, and among whom a special brotherhood prevails, which the Qur'an calls *wasiyyah* (mutual counsel).

Enjoining truth is necessary because carrying the truth is a difficult task; in this world there are countless factors that lead a person away from the path of truth: carnal desires, expediencies, national and family notions, the oppression of rebels and dictators, the injustice of oppressors, the transgressions and aggressions of those who exceed limits, and so on. By advising one another, in fact, reminders take place; people's resolve increases, and unity and harmony arise among the members of the group with respect to aims and objectives. And in bearing responsibilities, in fact, one carries another's burden. Through advice, all individual inclinations gather together and multiply many times over, and all those who are guardians and supporters of truth feel that they are not alone: in the task of protecting truth and righteousness there are others with them, who advise them, encourage them, love them, and stand behind them, and who will never let them be put to shame. This religion is indeed the truth, and only a community can protect this religion, a community that is mutually acquainted, mutually supportive, mutually helpful, and that makes up for one another's weaknesses.

And enjoining patience is also very necessary, because remaining on the path of faith and righteous action and watching over truth and justice is a difficult task. It requires patience, perseverance, and a fierce struggle against the factors within the self, and it also requires struggle against the factors outside the self, and there is need for endurance and hardship in the face of difficulties that come in this path. Likewise, it means being patient with the arrogance and pride of falsehood, being patient with the length of the road, being patient with the slowness of success, and with the effacement and disappearance of the signposts of the path, and being patient with them.

Through the enjoining of patience, human strength increases, and a collective feeling arises among people that all of us have a single goal and one direction; thus everyone finds a support in it. Workers, while working on this path, become close and united, and they advance with great resolve, steadfastness and insistence on their aim. Moreover, through it many other collective qualities also come into being, and these are necessary for the stability of an Islamic community, because Islam cannot live without a communal atmosphere. Islam's manifestation also takes the form of a society. If there is no society at all, Islam will not exist, and that would be a clear loss.

The Qur'an has set down for us a constitution by which a society is declared successful and protected from worldly and otherworldly loss. If we look at the present conditions of the world through the lens of this constitution, before us will appear this frightening picture of the world: that at this time the whole world is in complete loss. The more frightening aspect of this loss is that even before the Hereafter, we have fallen into severe loss from a purely worldly standpoint. We see that humanity has completely turned away from that goodness whose blessings and bounties Allah had made general for human beings. Moreover, from this world that sovereign authority has disappeared which is faithful and Islamic, which is founded upon the principles of goodness, truth and justice. The most unsightly aspect of this picture is that Muslims, or, to use more accurate words, those people who in comparison to the other inhabitants of this earth have fallen very far from that goodness and virtue, have gone very far from the system of life which Allah had chosen for them. They have trampled underfoot the constitution and law which Allah had prescribed for them, which Allah had declared to be the only path to salvation from loss and failure. Especially those regions from which the banners of this goodness were first raised: they themselves have brought down those banners which Allah had raised for them. These were the banners of faith. And the most unfortunate thing is that the regions from which the banners of Allah's religion were raised have adopted racial nationalism, although the history of this earth bears witness that through racial nationalism no nation has ever reached goodness. The racial nationalism (Arab nationalism) whose banners these people have raised existed among them even before Islam, but because of it they neither accomplished any notable feat on this earth, nor was any achievement of theirs recorded in the heavens. When Islam came, through the Arabs it raised a banner which was purely the banner of Allah; no other element shared in it. It was in the name of Allah; no one shared in the name; it was attributed to Allah alone, with no other attribution; it had only the colour of Allah and no other colour. Under the shade of this banner the Arabs attained ascendancy; they became the leaders of the world. And their leadership was the leadership of goodness: it was a strong leadership, a wise leadership, and a successful leadership from every aspect. This achievement succeeded for the first time in Arab history, and also in human history the Islamic revolution was a notable success for humanity.

Maulana Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in the chapter "Islamic Power and Muslim Leaders" of his famous book *Insani Duniya par Musalmanon ka Urooj-o-Zawal ka Asar* (The Effect of the Rise and Fall of the Muslims on the Human World), says:

"The Muslims came onto the field, took into their hands the reins of guiding the world, and removed from that office of guidance those sick nations which had seized it and which they had never used properly. The Muslims took the whole of humanity with them and began to lead it, with balance and right pace, toward its correct destination. In them were gathered all those qualities which proved them worthy of the exalted office of guiding all nations, and which, under their watch and leadership, guaranteed the welfare and felicity of nations. What were those distinctive qualities? They are these:

(1) They had the heavenly Book and the Shariah of God; they did not legislate on their own. For human legislation is a fountain of ignorance, oppression and error, and when humans make laws for humans, changes and amendments keep occurring in them every day, whereas heavenly books are protected from such errors. The Muslims were safe from blindly walking in their daily affairs, in politics and in leadership, and from groping in darkness. They had the light of divine revelation by which they walked, and by which all the paths and turns of life were lit for them. Every step they took fell in light, and they could clearly see their destination. In Surah al-An'am (6:122) it is said:

'Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, unable to emerge from it?'

They had a divine law and Shariah by which they judged between people. They were made standard-bearers of truth and justice, and they were commanded, even in the state of the strongest provocation, anger, enmity and hatred, not to abandon truth and justice, and not to take revenge in matters of truth and justice:

'O you who believe, be steadfast for Allah, witnesses in justice; and let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do' (5:8).

(2) They attained to rule and leadership after firm moral training and refinement of the soul. They did not leap from the depths to the heights with all the moral defects and flaws of the common ruling peoples of the world. Rather, for a long period divine revelation kept reforming and training them, and for years they were under the complete supervision and instruction of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He purified them and fully trained them. He made them accustomed to a life of asceticism and piety, and instilled in them chastity, trustworthiness, selflessness and sacrifice, and fear of God. He completely removed from their hearts greed and desire for rule and offices. His saying was: 'By God, we shall never entrust an office to one who asks for it or who desires it.' Their hearts were entirely purified of the wish for ascendancy, eminence and honour, and of the desire for strife and corruption; and in their ears, day and night, these words of the Qur'an resounded:

'That is the Abode of the Hereafter; We grant it to those who do not desire superiority on earth or corruption, and the best outcome is for the righteous' (28:83)."

If there is no such natural movement within it, that faith is counterfeit and dead faith. Faith is like a flower whose fragrance cannot be restrained: wherever there is a flower, its fragrance will continue to spread. And if a person has no scent of faith, then it is as though he does not exist.

From this it becomes clear that faith is the name of movement, action and construction, and all these matters are directed from Allah. There is no contraction in faith, nor is it a negative thing. Nor does it settle in the folds of conscience. Faith is not the name of good wishes that have no movement behind them. This is the open temperament of Islam, which makes Islam a lofty constructive force, and this power is the central driving force within practical life.

This is the meaning of the principle that faith must be connected with the Islamic system of life. The Islamic system of life, since it is the name of a continuous movement which is proceeding throughout this entire universe, and this movement has been created by a governing power, and it has a goal. Entrusting the leadership of humanity to faith means bringing into existence a leadership which produces a method of movement that is in accordance with the temperament of this entire universe; in other words, establishing a good, pure constructive struggle that is worthy of the system of life sent down by Allah.

*Wa tawasaw* ... *bi-al-sabr* (3:103): "who enjoin one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience." From the practice of enjoining truth and enjoining patience, the features of the Muslim community become clearly apparent. A united community (jama'ah muslimah) is also formed along the lines of the Muslim community. It has a distinct existence and personality. Its members have a distinctive bond among themselves. All people share one direction; this community or group has awareness of its own existence, and its duties are also before it, and this community knows what it has to do in respect of faith and righteous action; and it knows that it has to lead the whole of humanity from the standpoint of faith and righteous action. Therefore, enjoining one another to truth means that you must take up the great trust.

In short, from the word *tawasi* and from its meaning, its essence and its temperament, the existence of the Muslim community emerges, or the concept of a united community arises. That is, a community that is distinguished, wise, and responsible for establishing truth, goodness and justice on this earth. Thus this is the most exalted and beautiful picture of the Muslim community. Islam desires such a community: a distinguished, strong, wise community that watches over truth and goodness, whose members constantly advise one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience, who live together in mutual love and cooperation, and among whom a special brotherhood prevails, which the Qur'an calls *wasiyyah* (mutual counsel).

Enjoining truth is necessary because carrying the truth is a difficult task; in this world there are countless factors that lead a person away from the path of truth: carnal desires, expediencies, national and family notions, the oppression of rebels and dictators, the injustice of oppressors, the transgressions and aggressions of those who exceed limits, and so on. By advising one another, in fact, reminders take place; people's resolve increases, and unity and harmony arise among the members of the group with respect to aims and objectives. And in bearing responsibilities, in fact, one carries another's burden. Through advice, all individual inclinations gather together and multiply many times over, and all those who are guardians and supporters of truth feel that they are not alone: in the task of protecting truth and righteousness there are others with them, who advise them, encourage them, love them, and stand behind them, and who will never let them be put to shame. This religion is indeed the truth, and only a community can protect this religion, a community that is mutually acquainted, mutually supportive, mutually helpful, and that makes up for one another's weaknesses.

And enjoining patience is also very necessary, because remaining on the path of faith and righteous action and watching over truth and justice is a difficult task. It requires patience, perseverance, and a fierce struggle against the factors within the self, and it also requires struggle against the factors outside the self, and there is need for endurance and hardship in the face of difficulties that come in this path. Likewise, it means being patient with the arrogance and pride of falsehood, being patient with the length of the road, being patient with the slowness of success, and with the effacement and disappearance of the signposts of the path, and being patient with them.

Through the enjoining of patience, human strength increases, and a collective feeling arises among people that all of us have a single goal and one direction; thus everyone finds a support in it. Workers, while working on this path, become close and united, and they advance with great resolve, steadfastness and insistence on their aim. Moreover, through it many other collective qualities also come into being, and these are necessary for the stability of an Islamic community, because Islam cannot live without a communal atmosphere. Islam's manifestation also takes the form of a society. If there is no society at all, Islam will not exist, and that would be a clear loss.

The Qur'an has set down for us a constitution by which a society is declared successful and protected from worldly and otherworldly loss. If we look at the present conditions of the world through the lens of this constitution, before us will appear this frightening picture of the world: that at this time the whole world is in complete loss. The more frightening aspect of this loss is that even before the Hereafter, we have fallen into severe loss from a purely worldly standpoint. We see that humanity has completely turned away from that goodness whose blessings and bounties Allah had made general for human beings. Moreover, from this world that sovereign authority has disappeared which is faithful and Islamic, which is founded upon the principles of goodness, truth and justice. The most unsightly aspect of this picture is that Muslims, or, to use more accurate words, those people who in comparison to the other inhabitants of this earth have fallen very far from that goodness and virtue, have gone very far from the system of life which Allah had chosen for them. They have trampled underfoot the constitution and law which Allah had prescribed for them, which Allah had declared to be the only path to salvation from loss and failure. Especially those regions from which the banners of this goodness were first raised: they themselves have brought down those banners which Allah had raised for them. These were the banners of faith. And the most unfortunate thing is that the regions from which the banners of Allah's religion were raised have adopted racial nationalism, although the history of this earth bears witness that through racial nationalism no nation has ever reached goodness. The racial nationalism (Arab nationalism) whose banners these people have raised existed among them even before Islam, but because of it they neither accomplished any notable feat on this earth, nor was any achievement of theirs recorded in the heavens. When Islam came, through the Arabs it raised a banner which was purely the banner of Allah; no other element shared in it. It was in the name of Allah; no one shared in the name; it was attributed to Allah alone, with no other attribution; it had only the colour of Allah and no other colour. Under the shade of this banner the Arabs attained ascendancy; they became the leaders of the world. And their leadership was the leadership of goodness: it was a strong leadership, a wise leadership, and a successful leadership from every aspect. This achievement succeeded for the first time in Arab history, and also in human history the Islamic revolution was a notable success for humanity.

Maulana Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi, in the chapter "Islamic Power and Muslim Leaders" of his famous book *Insani Duniya par Musalmanon ka Urooj-o-Zawal ka Asar* (The Effect of the Rise and Fall of the Muslims on the Human World), says:

"The Muslims came onto the field, took into their hands the reins of guiding the world, and removed from that office of guidance those sick nations which had seized it and which they had never used properly. The Muslims took the whole of humanity with them and began to lead it, with balance and right pace, toward its correct destination. In them were gathered all those qualities which proved them worthy of the exalted office of guiding all nations, and which, under their watch and leadership, guaranteed the welfare and felicity of nations. What were those distinctive qualities? They are these:

(1) They had the heavenly Book and the Shariah of God; they did not legislate on their own. For human legislation is a fountain of ignorance, oppression and error, and when humans make laws for humans, changes and amendments keep occurring in them every day, whereas heavenly books are protected from such errors. The Muslims were safe from blindly walking in their daily affairs, in politics and in leadership, and from groping in darkness. They had the light of divine revelation by which they walked, and by which all the paths and turns of life were lit for them. Every step they took fell in light, and they could clearly see their destination. In Surah al-An'am (6:122) it is said:

'Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, unable to emerge from it?'

They had a divine law and Shariah by which they judged between people. They were made standard-bearers of truth and justice, and they were commanded, even in the state of the strongest provocation, anger, enmity and hatred, not to abandon truth and justice, and not to take revenge in matters of truth and justice:

'O you who believe, be steadfast for Allah, witnesses in justice; and let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do' (5:8).

(2) They attained to rule and leadership after firm moral training and refinement of the soul. They did not leap from the depths to the heights with all the moral defects and flaws of the common ruling peoples of the world. Rather, for a long period divine revelation kept reforming and training them, and for years they were under the complete supervision and instruction of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He purified them and fully trained them. He made them accustomed to a life of asceticism and piety, and instilled in them chastity, trustworthiness, selflessness and sacrifice, and fear of God. He completely removed from their hearts greed and desire for rule and offices. His saying was: 'By God, we shall never entrust an office to one who asks for it or who desires it.' Their hearts were entirely purified of the wish for ascendancy, eminence and honour, and of the desire for strife and corruption; and in their ears, day and night, these words of the Qur'an resounded:

'That is the Abode of the Hereafter; We grant it to those who do not desire superiority on earth or corruption, and the best outcome is for the righteous' (28:83)."
